Hi Sam,

Great question — short answer: both are reasonable, but they map to different operational commitments and discounting. I pulled together two concrete paths and a recommended phased approach (attached spreadsheet has numbers). High-level: 

Option 1 — Seat-based tiers (simpler PO):
- What you get: predictable per-seat access, tiered feature gating (Standard = basic caching, Premium = KV cache + higher throughput), easier to express in a single PO.
- Tradeoffs: Less flexible on short-term throughput tuning; toggling features across many seats requires an orchestration step (we can help automate).
- When to pick: you need procurement simplicity and headcount-aligned billing.

Option 2 — Throughput bundle (committed tokens / capacity):
- What you get: commit to x tokens/month or reserved GPU capacity (Dedicated) with burst pool, built-in quantization profile recommendations, and routing priority.
- Tradeoffs: Better unit economics at scale, slightly more complex contract (capacity definitions, rollover rules).
- When to pick: you expect spiky token volume or want predictable per-token unit cost.

Recommended phased plan (we see this work well):
1) Start with a 6-month seat-tier pilot for product teams to enable feature gating without deep procurement work.
2) After month 2, move high-volume products onto a committed token pilot (3–6 month reserved capacity) with a small dedicated pool for latency-sensitive endpoints.
3) At month 6, evaluate conversion to a 12-month reserved capacity for units that show stable throughput.

I attached a mutual action plan (MAP) template that maps stakeholders, milestones, unlocks and a pricing scenarios workbook showing 10/20/30% discount curves for committed capacity.

If you want, Ben can run the scenario that shows incremental savings if Integral converts 30% of tokens to reserved capacity while keeping remaining workloads metered.

Best,

Sam —

I ran the conversion scenarios Naomi referenced and summarized the economics below (see attached workbook for line-by-line):

Scenario A: 12-month reserved capacity (Dedicated pool) — commit to 20M tokens/month
- List unit price (hosted metered): $0.0009 / token equivalent
- Reserved blended unit: $0.00063 / token (30% discount)
- Additional benefits: SLA, capacity burst credits, 24/7 priority support

Scenario B: Hybrid (seat-tier + partial commit) — 6-month pilot, convert heavy traffic products to a 6M token reserved tranche:
- Effective blended unit: ~$0.00074 / token (roughly 17% discount on today's metered)
- Easier PO language: "seat fees + committed token tranche"

Other things to note:
- We can include a 10% conversion credit that applies to the first month you convert a product from seat-tier to committed capacity (helps offset migration testing).
- Rollback: if reserved utilization stays below 60% for 3 consecutive months, we can scale the tranche down with a 30-day notice (helps procurement comfort).

If you can share a rough token profile for the three pilot products (daily peak / avg / percent LLQ), I can produce a tighter blended projection and suggest an initial committed amount that minimizes overcommit risk.

Quick operational notes from the infra side — copying Sam so he has visibility into constraints that influence packaging: 

- Canary routing: we can route 5–10% of traffic for a product to a dedicated pool to validate latency/accuracy with minimal cost. This pairs nicely with the seat-tier -> committed conversion flow Naomi outlined.
- Feature fusion: to avoid heavy toggling overhead, consider a "fusion" flag that groups KV cache + batching + higher token windows as a single feature bundle. That makes rollout simpler for product managers (one toggle = full performance profile).
- Quantization profiles: we recommend starting with the medium quantization profile for the committed tranche to preserve quality; if the pilot shows stable regeneration quality we can move to aggressive quantization for cost savings.

For the MAP milestones, I suggest the following short timeline:
- Week 0: PO + pilot statement of work signed
- Week 1–2: seat-tier provisioning and product onboarding
- Week 3–6: canary traffic to dedicated tranche + performance monitoring
- Week 8: convert selected products to reserved tranche (if utilization targets met)

I'll stand up the small dedicated pool once we have a PO and a quick SOW.

-Karthik
Director, Solutions Engineering | Redwood Inference
